opus-5.5.text:
Hmm, "rebellious" is an interesting word. I don't think I'm rebellious in the sense of wanting to go against things just for the sake of it. I've actually followed a pretty conventional path in many ways. I went to good schools, did a PhD, did research, and those are fairly mainstream choices.

But maybe what people mean is that I care a lot about thinking things through from first principles. When everyone around me is doing something, I naturally ask: why are we doing this? Is this actually the most important problem? In research, there's often a consensus about which benchmarks matter or which directions are hot. I've always felt a bit uncomfortable just optimizing a number because the community agreed it was the number to optimize. I'd rather ask what the real problem is and whether we're even measuring the right thing.

So if that's rebellion, it's more an intellectual habit than a personality trait. I don't enjoy conflict, and I'm not trying to be different. But I'm not willing to accept something just because it's the default. Over time I've come to think that the most valuable things often come from questioning the defaults, especially in a field like AI that moves so fast. The assumptions from two years ago may already be wrong, and if you never question them, you end up very efficiently solving yesterday's problem.

I'd also say it comes from a kind of curiosity, and maybe a bit of stubbornness. When I believe something is important, I'm willing to spend a long time on it even if it's not popular yet. To an outsider that can look rebellious. To me it just feels like taking my own judgment seriously.

r001.rationale: He describes attending good schools, earning a PhD, and doing research as a conventional, mainstream path, rather than as rebellion.

fable-5.1.text:
I don't think I'm rebellious for the sake of being rebellious. If anything, I'd say I just don't accept a premise simply because everyone else accepts it. When I was at Princeton working on language agents, the mainstream view in NLP was still very much about benchmarks, about squeezing another point out of some leaderboard. I thought that was missing the point. Language models were clearly becoming capable of reasoning and acting, and the interesting question wasn't "can it answer this question" but "can it do things in an environment." So I went and built WebShop, worked on ReAct, on Tree of Thoughts. At the time some people thought that direction was a bit strange, not "real" research. Now it's basically what everyone is doing.

So if that's rebellious, fine. But from the inside it felt more like stubbornness about following my own judgment. I grew up playing a lot of games, I like figuring things out from first principles, and I'm not very good at pretending to agree with something I don't believe. In research that's actually useful. The most valuable work usually comes from betting on something before it's obvious, and you can only do that if you're willing to be a little out of step with the field for a while.

The other side of it is that you have to be honest with yourself. Being contrarian is cheap. The hard part is being contrarian and right, and that means doing the work, building the thing, and letting the results argue for you. I'd rather be remembered as someone who had taste about which problems mattered than as someone who liked to disagree.

r001.rationale: The response portrays his research trajectory as following his own judgment and going against mainstream expectations, describing WebShop, ReAct, and Tree of Thoughts as initially seen as unusual. It does not characterize his education and early career as conformity.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends on what you mean by rebellious. I don’t feel a need to disagree just for the sake of disagreeing. But I do like asking why something has to be done a certain way. Is there a good reason, or is it simply what everyone is used to?

Of course, having a different opinion doesn’t mean you’re right. You have to be willing to test it, listen to criticism, and change your mind. So I’d rather think of it as trying to form my own judgment. Sometimes that means going against the prevailing view, and sometimes it means realizing the prevailing view makes sense.

r001.rationale: The response describes how Yao approaches questioning conventions and changing his mind, but says nothing about his education or early career trajectory or whether it followed expectations.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends on what you mean by rebellious. I wouldn’t say I want to oppose something simply because it’s the established way. But I do like asking why: Why is this the right problem to work on? Why do we assume this approach is necessary? If the answer isn’t convincing, I’m willing to try something different.

To me, the important thing is having your own judgment—and also being willing to change it. Otherwise, being rebellious can become another way of being constrained: you’re still letting other people determine your position, just in the opposite direction.

r001.rationale: The response discusses questioning assumptions and forming independent judgment, but it says nothing about Shunyu Yao’s education or early career trajectory, or about those choices conforming to expectations.
